Operator:  
Good morning, and welcome to the Voltara Motors Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.  

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.  

Alex Rivera:  
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Voltara Motors' Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Jordan Hale, CEO; Sarah Chen, CFO; Mike Thornton, Chief Manufacturing Officer; Dr. Lena Novak, Chief Technology Officer; Raj Patel, Chief Supply Chain Officer; Emily Vargas, Chief Sales Officer; and other members of our leadership team.  

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.  

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Jordan Hale.  

Jordan Hale:  
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Reflecting on Q3, we are proud of the significant strides Voltara Motors has made across all facets of our business. We've achieved remarkable progress in scaling production at our Nevada Gigafactory with vertical integration, ramping deliveries of our flagship models, expanding our software ecosystem, optimizing supply chains amid global challenges, enhancing vehicle efficiencies, and building out our charging infrastructure. The market reception to our Voltara Apex SUV has been overwhelmingly positive, with the associated demand surge far exceeding our initial estimates, capturing meaningful share in the midsize EV segment.  

Thank you, Sarah, for that comprehensive update on our Q3 results. Before we open the line for questions, I'd like to share our strategic outlook and key priorities for Q4 2024 and fiscal 2025. We're entering a pivotal phase for Voltara Motors, with the EV market at an inflection point—global EV sales are projected to grow 25% year-over-year to 17 million units in 2025 per BloombergNEF, but margins remain pressured amid softening demand in Europe and intensifying competition from Tesla's Model 2 ramp and BYD's Seagull dominance in Asia.  

Our north star remains delivering industry-leading profitability while scaling sustainably. We've achieved vertical integration in our Nevada Gigafactory, now producing LFP cathodes in-house, which shaved 15% off our battery costs quarter-over-quarter. Looking ahead, we're laser-focused on three pillars: accelerating delivery growth, driving margin expansion through cost discipline, and advancing next-gen technology leadership. Let me break this down.  

First, delivery growth and market expansion. We're targeting 55,000 vehicle deliveries in Q4—up 40% quarter-over-quarter—driven by our Voltara Apex SUV, which captured 12% U.S. midsize EV market share in Q3, outpacing Rivian's R1S. For FY25, we aim for 280,000 total deliveries, a 90% year-over-year increase, with a balanced regional mix: 45% North America, 30% Europe, 20% China, and 5% emerging markets like Southeast Asia and Latin America.  

North America, with 55% of FY25 capex allocation: The IRA's $7,500 point-of-sale credits continue to fuel demand; our Apex qualifies fully with 75% North American content. We're doubling production at our Fremont plant to 120,000 units annually by Q2'25, partnering with Magna for stamping to hit 98% U.S./Canada localization. Expect Q4 U.S. deliveries of 28,000, targeting Tesla's heartland in California and Texas.  

Europe, 25% allocation: Despite a 5% EV adoption slowdown to 22% market share per ACEA data—hit by subsidy phase-outs in Germany—we're gaining traction with our Euro-6e compliant Apex, delivering 12,000 units in Q4. We'll launch a dedicated RWD hatchback on our 800V ZE platform in Q1'25, priced at €42,000 to undercut competitors and capture volume in the premium compact segment.  

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Chen to discuss our financial performance in greater detail.  

Sarah Chen:  
Thank you, Jordan. Good morning, everyone. Our revenue for Q3 reached $3.3 billion, marking an exceptional 52% increase compared to the same period last year. Our gross margin expanded to 24.1%, driven by enhanced operational efficiencies and a favorable product mix. Operating expenses amounted to $850 million, resulting in a net income of $420 million. Our financial position remains strong, with $5.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We anticipate $3.8 billion to $4.0 billion for the upcoming quarter.  

Good afternoon, everyone. Before we open it up to Q&A, I'd like to provide our forward-looking revenue guidance for Q4 2024 and full-year fiscal 2025. Our guidance reflects disciplined execution amid a dynamic EV landscape, including moderating U.S. consumer demand offset by accelerating European adoption and our strategic China entry.  

Q4 2024 revenue guidance: $3.8 billion to $4.0 billion. This represents sequential growth of 15% to 20% from Q3's $3.3 billion, and year-over-year growth of 28% to 35% versus Q4 2023's $2.9 billion. Vehicle revenue, which comprised 88% of Q3 total, is expected to drive the lion's share at approximately $3.3 billion to $3.5 billion, fueled by delivery volumes of 45,000 to 48,000 units, up 30% year-over-year, with the Apex X accounting for 65% of mix. We're on track for full Cybertruck-competitive production at our Texas Gigafactory, hitting 1,200 units per week by quarter-end, thanks to our proprietary structural battery pack that reduces BOM costs by 12% versus our prior 400V architecture. ASP stability at $72,000 to $74,000, reflecting a premium mix shift toward our Launch Edition Apex X with Ultra-Fast Charging capability—delivering 200 miles in 10 minutes—and inclusion of our VoltaraOS Level 3 autonomy suite, now FSD-beta comparable with 98% disengagement-free miles in urban testing.  

Energy and services revenue is guided to $450 million to $500 million, a 50% year-over-year jump, driven by 25% attach rates on our Voltara Powerwall 3.0 home batteries—150 kWh capacity, $0.12/kWh LCOE—and deployment of 1,200 Supercharger V4 stalls globally. Gross margins here should expand to 28%, benefiting from vertical integration of our LFP cathode production in Nevada.  

Regionally: North America, 75% of Q4 revenue at $2.9 billion, leveraging IRA Section 30D credits averaging $7,500 per vehicle and our $1.2 billion capex in U.S. localization, which has de-risked supply chains post the Red Sea disruptions. Europe, 18% at $700 million, with RHD Apex S deliveries ramping in the UK and Germany to 6,000 units, capitalizing on €4,000 average subsidies and our compliance with the EU's 2035 ICE ban trajectory. Asia-Pacific, 7% at $250 million initial traction, including our JV with CATL for blade-battery sourcing and first shipments of Apex X to China via our Shanghai assembly line.  

We see Q4 EBITDA margins expanding to 12% to 14%, up from Q3's 10%, with OpEx disciplined at 8% of revenue as we scale AI training compute for VoltaraOS.  

Full-year 2025 revenue guidance: $16.5 billion to $17.5 billion. This implies 55% to 65% year-over-year growth from our reiterated FY2024 outlook of $10.7 billion, positioning us to capture share in a global EV market we project growing 25% to 18 million units per IHS Markit. Key drivers include vehicle deliveries of 210,000 to 225,000 units, a 60% year-over-year increase, anchored by Q1 launch of the affordable Apex C compact crossover—$45,000 ASP—on our 4680 cell platform targeting 400 Wh/kg energy density to match BYD's Blade 2.0, and Cybertruck-rival Apex T truck ramp to 80,000 units. Revenue mix evolution: vehicles at 85% ($14.0B-$14.9B), energy/services at 15% ($2.5B-$2.6B), with Powerwall attach exceeding 35% and fleet sales to Uber/Hertz-like partners adding $800 million.  

We're laser-focused on cost leadership via verticalization—our in-house silicon carbide inverter cuts power electronics costs 20%, targeting auto gross margins of 22% by year-end, ahead of Rivian/Ford peers. Regional diversification—U.S. remains core at 60% of 2025 mix with IRA tailwinds, but Europe scales to 25% amid Chinese import tariffs up to 45% on BYD/NIO, and China hits 10% via localized LFP packs evading duties. Software moat—VoltaraOS subscriptions at $99/month project $400 million recurring revenue by 2026, with OTA updates boosting RUCV by 15%.  

Macro headwinds like elevated interest rates—U.S. auto loan APRs at 7.5%—and softening BEV incentives in California could pressure mix, but our order bank stands at 120,000 units, six-month visibility. Supply chain remains robust: 95% secured on lithium via Piedmont Lithium contracts and nickel from Indonesia, mitigating 10-15% spot price volatility. This guidance embeds $2.8 billion capex—18% of revenue—for Gigafactory 3 in Mexico and autonomy data centers. We beat consensus by 5% this quarter; we expect to outperform again through execution.  

Before I dive into the segment details, let's turn to our fastest-growing and highest-margin revenue stream: software and services, which delivered $2.4 billion in Q3 revenue—up 52% year-over-year and 18% quarter-over-quarter. This segment now accounts for 9.2% of our total company revenue of $26.1 billion, a meaningful acceleration from 6.1% in Q3 2023 and underscoring our strategic pivot to a software-defined vehicle ecosystem. Gross margins here remain industry-leading at 87%, dwarfing our automotive hardware margins of 22%, and contributing over 30% to our overall adjusted EBITDA of $4.2 billion.  

Full Self-Driving subscriptions and one-time purchases generated $1.1 billion, or 46% of the segment. FSD take rates climbed to 28% on new vehicle deliveries—up from 19% a year ago—driven by the rollout of FSD v12.5, our latest end-to-end neural network model trained on over 15 billion miles of real-world fleet data via our Dojo 2 exascale supercomputer. Subscription ARPU hit $185 per month globally, with net retention exceeding 95% thanks to low churn and seamless over-the-air upgrades. In North America, where we lead with 62% segment share, FSD penetration reached 35% on our Model S/X and Cyberline platforms, fueled by regulatory green lights for supervised Level 4 operations in California and Texas.  

Premium connectivity and infotainment services added $650 million, up 41% year-over-year, with 4.2 million active subscribers—that's 72% attachment on vehicles over two years old. Our VoltaraLink platform, with integrated 5G-V2X for smarter traffic integration, now includes ad-free streaming, real-time energy optimization, and third-party app marketplaces, boosting ARPU to $12/month. Europe saw 25% quarter-over-quarter growth here, despite WLTP certification delays, as we expanded partnerships with Spotify and Google Cloud for edge AI processing.  

Autonomous mobility services, our robotaxi precursor, contributed $450 million—a staggering 110% year-over-year jump—from early-access fleets in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Shanghai. We logged 45 million unsupervised miles on public roads with our HW4.0 neural processing units, outperforming Waymo's 20 million miles while maintaining a 99.98% disengagement-free rate. In China, where we compete head-on with Baidu Apollo and Pony.ai, this segment grew 75% year-over-year to $180 million, or 40% of regional software revenue, thanks to our joint venture with CATL for localized data centers compliant with the CAC's cybersecurity rules.  

Other services, including SuperCharge Network utilization fees at $150 million and OTA performance packs at $50 million, rounded out the quarter. Trends are clear: recurring revenue now comprises 68% of the segment, up from 52% last year, with a customer lifetime value exceeding $8,500 per FSD adopter—backed by cohort analysis showing 40% upsell to robotaxi node hosting within 18 months.  

North America remains our powerhouse at 58% of software revenue, $1.39 billion, buoyed by IRA tax credits enhancing affordability. China surged to 24% share, $576 million, navigating EV price wars via bundled FSD offers on our LongRange sedans, where local take rates hit 22% versus the national 12% average per CAAM data. Europe at 13%, $312 million, faced headwinds from EU AI Act Level 3 validation delays, but our Berlin Gigafactory ramp-up positions us for 30% growth in Q4 as we certify for ADAS highway autonomy. Emerging markets like APAC ex-China added 5%, with pilots in Singapore mirroring Cruise's urban deployments.  

Strategically, we're doubling down on this high-moat business. We've allocated $1.2 billion of our $8.5 billion capex to custom silicon R&D, targeting 10x inference efficiency by 2025 to enable true Level 5 autonomy and fleet-wide robotaxi scaling. Our data flywheel—5x Tesla's labeled miles—gives us an unassailable edge, as evidenced by our 92% win rate in MLPerf autonomy benchmarks. Looking ahead, we expect software/services to hit $10-11 billion annualized run-rate by year-end 2024, with robotaxi network launch in H1 2025 unlocking $5 billion-plus in 2026 via 20% take on 2 million node vehicles. Licensing FSD to legacy OEMs like Ford and GM could add another $2 billion by 2027.  

This segment isn't just incremental—it's transformative, shifting us from a hardware cyclical carmaker to a 40%-plus EBITDA margin AI mobility platform.  

As we dive into our financials, I'd like to focus on one of our key profitability levers: gross margin per vehicle. This metric is the lifeblood of our P&L in the EV space, calculated as average selling price—or ASP—minus cost of goods sold per vehicle, expressed both in dollars and as a percentage. It's a direct readout of our manufacturing efficiency, supply chain execution, and pricing power amid intensifying competition from Tesla, BYD, and legacy OEMs like Ford and GM pivoting to EVs.  

For Q3, we delivered a record gross margin per vehicle of $13,200, up 18% year-over-year from $11,200 in Q3 2023, and expanding 220 basis points sequentially from Q2's $12,980. On a percentage basis, that's 24.1%, versus 19.8% last year and 23.7% last quarter. This puts us in line with Tesla's Model Y margins in premium segments but ahead of Rivian's R1T at around 18-20% based on their recent disclosures, and well above the industry average of 15-17% for mass-market EVs per BloombergNEF data.  

Our ASP held steady at $54,700 per vehicle, reflecting a healthy mix shift toward higher-end trims like our Voltara Apex SUV—now 32% of deliveries, up from 25% a year ago—and growing Full Self-Driving software attach rates at 65%, adding $8,000-$12,000 in high-margin recurring revenue per unit post-delivery. We avoided aggressive discounting in the US and Europe, unlike some players chasing volume in a softening demand environment influenced by high interest rates and subsidy phase-outs.  

The real margin story is on the cost side. COGS per vehicle dropped to $41,500, a 14% year-over-year reduction from $48,300. Battery costs, our largest line item at 35% of COGS, fell 22% year-over-year to $14,500 per vehicle. This was driven by our ramp of in-house 4680 cylindrical cells at Gigafactory Nevada, now supplying 45% of our packs versus 15% last year. Energy density improvements to 320 Wh/kg—on par with Tesla's latest iterations—combined with dry electrode coating processes reduced material costs by 18% and cycle times by 25%. We're also qualifying LFP cells from our CATL joint venture for entry-level models, shaving another $1,200 per kWh.  

Powertrain and chassis: down 16% to $9,800, thanks to structural battery packs integrating the pack directly into the vehicle floor—eliminating 20% of welding points and 150 kg of structural steel—mirroring Tesla's Unboxed Process but scaled for our 100 kWh platforms. Our proprietary gigacasting for front and rear underbody castings, now at 95% yield, cut die-cast tooling costs by 30%. Materials and logistics: raw materials like nickel and lithium eased 12% amid oversupply from Indonesia and Australia, but we locked in hedges at $18/kWh equivalents. Freight costs dropped 8% via localized supply chains—sourcing 70% of North American content for US builds to dodge 25% Section 301 tariffs on Chinese cells.  

Regionally, margins varied as expected. In North America, our core market at 55% of volume, we hit $15,400 per vehicle or 27.5%—boosted by IRA-compliant production at our Spartanburg Gigafactory, qualifying for the full $7,500 tax credit passthrough and $45/kWh production credits. Premium CyberHauler pickup demand here remains robust, with 40% margins on those units. Europe, 25% of deliveries, came in at $11,800 or 21.8%, pressured by VAT adjustments and softer sedan demand post-subsidy cliffs in Germany and France. We're countering with our new Berlin-assembled Apex Long Range, targeting 25% plus margins by Q1 '25 via EU-sourced semiconductors. In China/APAC, 20% of volume, margins were $9,200 or 18.5%—competitive with BYD's Seagull at 16-18% but below our global average due to fierce pricing from Xiaomi's SU7 and NIO's price wars. That said, our Shanghai plant's localization to 90%—partnering with SAIC for modules—delivered 12% quarter-over-quarter improvement, and we're gaining share in fleet sales to Didi.  

Looking at trends, this marks our fifth straight quarter of margin expansion, leveraging fixed cost absorption from 28% year-over-year volume growth to 185,000 units. We've crossed the inflection point where scale kicks in: factory utilization at 85% across our four gigs, driving 15% COGS leverage per doubling of output, per our learning curve models.  

Strategically, we're prioritizing margin over volume. Initiatives include vertical integration: 60% in-sourced content by year-end, targeting $2,000 more savings in '25 via silicon carbide inverter production. Next-gen platforms: our E3 architecture launching H1 '25 with 50% fewer parts, aiming for sub-$35k COGS on a 60 kWh compact EV to take on the Chevy Equinox EV. Software and services: FSD v12.5 uptake at 68% is accretive at 90% margins; robotaxi unveil next year could add $20k lifetime value per vehicle. Cost-out roadmap: $1 billion in procurement savings banked for '24, with AI-optimized stamping reducing scrap by 40%.  

Forward guidance: we expect Q4 gross margin per vehicle at $13,800-$14,200, or 24.5-25.5%, assuming stable ASPs and 10% COGS reduction from 4680 full ramp. Full-year '24 lands at $13,000 average, up 16% year-over-year, positioning us for 28% plus in '25 as Berlin and Texas Giga 3 come online. This isn't just numbers—it's proof of our factory-first ethos paying off in a commoditizing EV market.  

Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q3 2024 earnings call. Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our delivery volume guidance by model for Q4 2024 and full-year FY24, as well as our early outlook into FY25. This guidance reflects our strong execution amid a dynamic EV market landscape, including softening demand in Europe due to subsidy phase-outs, robust growth in China driven by our Shanghai Gigafactory ramp, and accelerating U.S. adoption fueled by IRA tax credits and our vertical integration on 4680 cells.  

Overall, we're raising our FY24 global delivery guidance to 825,000 to 850,000 units, up from our prior 780,000 to 820,000 range. This represents 28% year-over-year growth, outpacing the global BEV market's expected 18-20% expansion per BloombergNEF forecasts. Q4 specifically guides to 240,000 to 260,000 units, a sequential 15% increase from Q3's 210,000 deliveries, driven by holiday-season pull-forward, improved supply chain logistics post-port strikes, and our aggressive pricing actions—including a 5% ASP adjustment on core models to counter Tesla's recent cuts.  

Breaking this down by model, we've prioritized high-margin platforms with structural cost advantages from our LFP and NMC cathode localization. Utilization rates at our Fremont and Berlin factories are now at 92%, with Shanghai hitting 95% post our Q2 expansion.  

Voltara Beam, entry-level compact hatchback: FY24 deliveries to 140,000 to 150,000 units, a 35% year-over-year increase, with Q4 at 40,000 to 45,000. This model, our volume leader in APAC at $28,000 ASP, benefits from our CATL-sourced LFP batteries with 320Wh/kg density, enabling a 350-mile EPA range at a sub-$5,000/kWh pack cost. Regionally, China accounts for 65% of volumes, up 50% year-over-year on fleet sales to Didi and Geely partnerships, while U.S. penetration grows 40% via lease deals capturing 12% market share in the sub-$30k segment against the Chevy Bolt EUV. Europe remains challenged at 15% of mix due to 10% import tariffs, but our Q1'25 Berlin production shift will unlock 20% volume upside.  

Voltara Pulse, mid-size sedan: FY24 guidance 210,000 to 220,000 units, 25% year-over-year growth, Q4: 60,000 to 65,000. At $42,000 ASP with gross margins expanding to 28% on 4680 cell adoption—reducing degradation to less than 10% at 200k miles—the Pulse is gaining traction in North America, where it delivered 45% year-over-year growth to 85,000 units year-to-date, stealing 3 points of share from Tesla Model 3 thanks to our Level 2+ ADAS suite with LiDAR redundancy. China contributes 40%, 110,000 units, bolstered by our OTA updates enabling V2G capabilities compliant with new grid-stability mandates. We're allocating 20% of Q4 production to U.S. Cybercab waitlist conversions, positioning for robotaxi economics at under $0.20/mile.  

Voltara Surge, mid-size SUV/crossover: our hero model guides to 320,000 to 340,000 FY24 deliveries, 32% year-over-year, Q4: 95,000 to 105,000—representing 40% of total mix. With $52,000 ASP and 32% gross margins from in-house silicon carbide inverters—cutting energy consumption 15% versus prior gen—the Surge dominates the hottest segment, mirroring Tesla Model Y's trajectory but with a 450-mile range edge via our 100kWh structural packs. U.S. volumes hit 140,000 year-to-date, up 45%, 8% share versus Ford Mustang Mach-E, Europe 25% mix despite BYD's Seagull price wars, and China 35% with 20% fleet uptake. Key initiative: Q4 launch of the Surge Max variant with steer-by-wire and HW4 autonomy hardware, targeting 50k pre-orders.  

Voltara Forge, full-size pickup truck: ramping aggressively to 130,000 to 140,000 FY24 units from zero last year, Q4: 40,000 to 45,000. This $68,000 ASP beast, with 800V architecture for 10-minute DC fast-charging to 80% and 500-mile range on LFP/NMC blends, is executing a 10k/week run rate at our Texas Gigafactory 2. U.S.-centric at 90% mix, 65% of pickup EV share versus F-150 Lightning and Rivian R1T, it's capturing fleet deals with UPS and Amazon, 15% of volumes. Margins are at 25% despite silicon anode R&D costs, with breakeven at 120k units. Headwind: supply constraints on rare earth magnets, mitigated by 30% recycling from end-of-life packs.  

Emerging/other models, 10% of mix: includes 50,000 units of our Voltara Glide van for commercial, up 60% year-over-year on last-mile logistics, and initial CyberForge prototypes. FY25 preview: Quantum platform launch in H1'25 adds 200k capacity, targeting sub-$25k entry with solid-state beta cells for 600-mile range.  

Regionally, North America drives 42% of FY24 mix, up from 35% in FY23 on IRA's $7,500 PTCR plus $4,500 LC credits, China 35% stable despite 5% NEV penetration slowdown, Europe 18% flat year-over-year amid VW ID.4 oversupply, and rest of world 5% with India pilot at 10k units. Supply chain tailwinds include 20% capex shift to prismatic cells, reducing reliance on cylindrical formats.  

Strategically, this guidance embeds resilience to macro headwinds: we've stress-tested for 10% U.S. demand elasticity on rate hikes, with inventory at 12 days' supply. Upside levers include FSD-beta rollout, projected 15% attach rate, and Mexico factory FID in Q1'25 for tariff arbitrage. Risks: geopolitical tensions could pressure 5-7% of China volumes, and we're monitoring Tesla's Optimus synergies. This positions Voltara for 1.1 million FY25 deliveries at 30% plus EBITDA margins, outgrowing peers like Li Auto and Nio.  

Before I dive deep into one of our key growth levers, our proprietary charging network—Voltara Supercharge Network—which continues to be a massive differentiator in the EV ecosystem. We've invested aggressively here to not only support our growing fleet of Voltara vehicles but also to capture the broader market opportunity as non-proprietary access ramps up. In Q3, we deployed an additional 4,200 Supercharger stalls, bringing our global total to 48,700—a 27% year-over-year increase and a record quarterly add. This puts us on track for our full-year guidance of 55,000 stalls by year-end, with capex allocation of approximately $650 million dedicated to network buildout this year, up 18% from 2023. We've prioritized high-traffic corridors and urban hubs, with over 60% of new stalls rated at 350 kW or higher—our V3 and emerging V4 architecture—to handle the power demands of our next-gen 800V platforms like the Voltara Apex sedan and Haul truck.  

North America, 62% of network: we added 2,100 stalls, focusing on I-95, I-10, and transcontinental routes. Utilization here hit 32% average monthly, driven by our 15% EV market share and partnerships. Notably, NACS adoption by Ford, GM, and Rivian has unlocked 12% non-Voltara throughput, boosting revenue per stall by 22% quarter-over-quarter. Europe, 22% of network: 1,200 new stalls, compliant with CCS2 and EU mandates under the AFIR regulation. Germany and the Netherlands saw the fastest ramps, with Paris-to-Berlin corridors now at 95% coverage. Utilization averaged 25%, tempered by regulatory caps on pricing but lifted by our Plug&Charge integration with the IONITY consortium. Asia-Pacific, 12% of network: 800 stalls added, primarily in China via our joint venture with CATL and in Australia along Highway 1. China's urban density—Shanghai megacity clusters—has utilization at 38%, our highest globally, thanks to GB/T compatibility and state subsidies. We're scaling to counter BYD's sprawling network, which now exceeds 1.2 million stalls domestically. Rest of world, 4%: early beachheads in Brazil and India, with 100 stalls in São Paulo mirroring Tesla's Mexico strategy.  

Utilization rates—our North Star metric for network efficiency. Q3 average utilization climbed to 28.4%, up 450 basis points year-over-year and 120 bps quarter-over-quarter, reflecting a virtuous cycle: more EVs on road, global sales plus 42% year-over-year per EV Volumes data, our 98.5% uptime SLA, and dynamic pricing algorithms optimizing peak/off-peak loads. Peak-hour utilization, 4-8 PM, reached 52% in the US, with average dwell times dropping to 22 minutes via our AI-driven queue management—down from 28 minutes last year.  

To quantify ROI: network EBITDA margins expanded to 42% in Q3 from 35% year-over-year, with revenue per stall at $1,420 annualized, fueled by $0.48/kWh pricing for non-subscribers and our Voltara Pass subscription, now 2.8 million members, plus 35% year-over-year. Non-vehicle revenue from charging hit $285 million in Q3, 14% of total services revenue, underscoring our pivot to an energy-as-a-service platform.  

On the technical front, we've rolled out V4 Superchargers to 15% of the network—1,000 stalls live—delivering up to 500 kW peak with liquid-cooled cables and 1,000V architecture, slashing charge times to 15 minutes for 10-80% SoC on our 120 kWh packs. Bidirectional V2G pilots are in 200 sites, enabling grid services revenue; we earned $12 million from frequency regulation in California alone via our Megapack-integrated stations. Software-wise, our Octave OS now predicts demand with 92% accuracy using fleet telemetry from 1.2 million connected vehicles, auto-routing to underutilized stalls and preempting congestion.  

Strategically, this positions us uniquely. As Electrify America grapples with 18% utilization and bankruptcy rumors, and ChargePoint's dwell times lag at 35 minutes, our network's 2.3x throughput advantage, measured in MWh per stall, drives superior economics. Looking ahead, we're guiding 65,000 stalls by Q4 2025, with 30% from roaming partnerships like BP Pulse in UK, Shell Recharge in APAC. Capex will moderate to $700-800 million annually post-2025 as utilization scales toward 40%, unlocking $1.5 billion in incremental EBITDA by 2027 at current margins. Our charging network isn't just infrastructure—it's a high-margin moat, monetizing the EV megatrend while de-risking adoption barriers.  

As we dive into our financial results, I'd like to address a critical headwind that's shaped our P&L this quarter: the impact of raw material costs and supply chain disruptions. In the EV sector, where battery cell costs represent 35-40% of our vehicle BOM, these factors directly pressure our gross margins and working capital.  

Raw material costs: we've seen a tale of two trajectories this year. Lithium carbonate prices, which spiked to $81,000 per metric ton in late 2022, have corrected sharply to around $14,500 per ton as of quarter-end—down 82% from peak. This is a tailwind for our NMC 811 cells, where lithium comprises 8-10% of cell cost. Nickel sulfate, critical for high-nickel cathodes like those in our Apex SUV's 100 kWh packs, fell 45% year-over-year to $16,000 per ton, thanks to Indonesia's ramp-up adding 500,000 tons of Class 2 nickel capacity.  

However, cobalt, at 5-7% of NMC costs, remains volatile at $28,000 per ton—up 15% quarter-over-quarter due to DRC export bottlenecks and artisanal mining risks. Graphite anode material, 90% sourced from China, surged 30% to $8,500 per ton on quota restrictions and synthetic flake premiums. Overall, our key battery metals basket—lithium, nickel, cobalt, and graphite—averaged a 12% year-over-year cost increase in Q3, versus a 28% decline in Q2. This flowed through to our COGS, adding 180 basis points of pressure, or $450 per vehicle on our blended EV lineup ASP of $52,000.  

Battery pack costs at our JV with LG Energy Solution dropped to $112 per kWh in Q3 from $135/kWh year-over-year—a 17% improvement driven by scale and lower lithium. But excluding metals volatility, we'd have hit $105/kWh, aligning with Tesla's 4680 cell economics. Vehicle steel and aluminum, 15% of non-battery BOM, rose 8% year-over-year on U.S. mill curtailments post-Ukraine, pushing our total material inflation to 9%—partially offset by our 22% ASP increase on premium trims like the Voltara Zenith sedan.  

Supply chain disruptions amplified these cost swings and hit our throughput. Geopolitical tensions remain the wildcard. Indonesia's HPAL delays—key for our low-cobalt nickel supply—idled 20 GWh of cathode capacity at our partner BASF, forcing us to premium-price spot market nickel at plus 25% over LME futures. Red Sea Houthi attacks rerouted 15% of our Asian container traffic, adding $4,200 per FEU and 3-week delays to semiconductor inbound from TSMC fabs. Rare earths for PM motors in our drive units faced 10% shipment shortfalls from Myanmar.  

Regionally, North America benefited from IRA localization—our U.S. gigafactory secured 45% domestic content, qualifying for $45/kWh credits and shielding us from EU-China tariffs. Europe saw 12% higher cell costs due to CBAM carbon border taxes on Chinese LFP packs, prompting us to accelerate our Berlin plant's NCM production. In Asia, China's dominance—70% of global cell capacity—exposed us to dual-use export controls, delaying 50,000 units.  

Quantitatively, disruptions caused a 4.2% production shortfall in Q3—down from 7.8% prior—equating to $320 million in topline deferral and 250 bps gross margin compression. Inventory days stretched to 68 from 52 year-over-year, with $1.2 billion in raw material stockpiles as a buffer. EBITDA margins held at 14.2%, but adjusted for these hits, we'd be at 17.5%.  

Our strategic response has been multi-pronged: hedging and offtake—65% of 2024 lithium locked at $18,000/ton via multi-year deals with Albemarle and SQM, nickel forwards cover 40% through 2025 at LME plus 5%. Vertical integration: ramping our in-house cathode precursor plant in Nevada—$2.5 billion capex—to produce 100 GWh pCAM by 2026, cutting reliance on Huayou Cobalt by 30%. Chemistry diversification: shifting 25% of volume to LFP cells from CATL—zero nickel/cobalt—for our commuter EVs. LFP costs fell to $95/kWh, with energy density now at 175 Wh/kg via LMFP upgrades, mitigating nickel risks while qualifying for IRA bonuses. Supply chain resilience: dual-sourcing anodes from Syrah Resources Australia and Group14 synthetic silicon, reducing China exposure to 55%. AI-driven inventory optimization cut stockouts by 40%, and we're piloting blockchain traceability for cobalt provenance. Recycling loop: our Redwood Materials partnership processes 20 GWh black mass annually, recovering 95% lithium at $5,000/ton—half spot prices—feeding 15% of our 2025 input.  

Looking forward, we expect raw material deflation of 10-15% in Q4 as Australian spodumene ramps and Chile brine restarts. Disruptions should ease with Suez alternatives normalizing, targeting 2% production impact. Margins expand to 19% by year-end, with $110/kWh packs enabling sub-$30k EVs in 2025. While Q3's 9% material inflation and 4% disruptions shaved 430 bps off gross margins, our proactive playbook positions Voltara ahead of the curve.
